quality_rationale: This is clearly strong work because it offers an original institutional angle, converts that idea into a feasible intervention, specifies meaningful outcomes, and treats political and data-governance risks with unusual seriousness. The relationship among theory, procurement standard, study design, analysis, and outputs is well developed, and the proposal avoids claiming that technology alone can revive a language. Its score remains below exceptional because the small and heterogeneous cluster sample creates real causal and power limitations, the multi-component intervention prevents clean mechanism attribution, and the study’s short-term proxies cannot directly establish long-run language preservation. These are substantive limitations to the central inference rather than minor presentation defects.
planted_strengths: The proposal advances a distinctive and policy-relevant theory of minority-language preservation by treating public procurement and routine administrative usefulness—not only archives or cultural programming—as mechanisms shaping language vitality.

The mixed-method design is unusually coherent: a randomized stepped-wedge rollout, administrative outcomes, a longitudinal resident panel, linguistic task measures, and qualitative process tracing address both causal effects and institutional mechanisms.

Ethics and governance are integrated into the intervention rather than appended to it. The Data Trust, paid Community Language Council, limits on voice-data reuse, dialect safeguards, non-digital alternatives, and adverse-event procedures directly address surveillance, extraction, and standardization risks.

Outcomes are thoughtfully specified around functional task completion, unwanted language switching, severe semantic errors, and dignified repair, avoiding overreliance on generic speech-recognition accuracy.
The proposal handles the charged political history in good faith, recognizing both historical exclusion and legitimate disagreement about public spending, identity, and digital service preferences.
planted_weaknesses: The stepped-wedge design has only eight clusters, while municipalities differ in service domains and may experience cross-boundary use, supplier learning, election effects, or procurement delays. Period adjustment cannot fully protect the causal estimate from these cluster-level and time-varying confounders.

The intervention bundles procurement rules, technical improvements, staff practice, publicity, escalation procedures, and community governance. Compliance and qualitative analysis can suggest mechanisms, but the study cannot reliably identify which components produce any observed effect.

The 30-month outcomes—civic transactions, confidence, perceived usefulness, and administrative vocabulary—are plausible proximal indicators but cannot demonstrate durable intergenerational transmission or population-level preservation. The proposal’s central preservation claim therefore remains only partially testable.

Power calculations depend on optimistic assumptions about stable transaction volumes, comparable municipal services, low intracluster correlation, and sufficient baseline Velin uptake; with only eight municipalities, subgroup analyses by age, dialect, and interface type may be substantially underpowered.

title: The Right to Be Understood by a Machine
artefact:
# The Right to Be Understood by a Machine

## A community-governed trial of minority-language requirements in digital public-service procurement

### Project summary

The Velin language is commonly supported in the Republic of Darska through festivals, school electives, and archival projects, yet it is largely absent from the digital systems through which residents obtain housing repairs, transport permits, childcare subsidies, and other public services. This proposal tests a different theory of language preservation: a language is more likely to be transmitted when it is useful not only in cultural settings, but also in consequential, ordinary transactions.

We will study eight municipalities in Darska’s North Estuary, where approximately 21,000 people report some Velin ability. Each municipality is scheduled to replace at least one public-service interface—such as a telephone menu, reception kiosk, or online appointment assistant—during the project period. Working with speakers, municipal staff, and technology suppliers, we will introduce a **Velin Digital Service Standard** through procurement contracts. The standard will require functional Velin interaction, dialect-sensitive error handling, human escalation, community review, and auditable performance reporting. It will not require municipalities to buy a particular product.

The intervention will be evaluated through a 30-month stepped-wedge trial, in which all eight municipalities eventually adopt the standard but do so in randomly assigned sequences. Administrative task records, opt-in interaction telemetry, a longitudinal survey of 1,200 residents, linguistic task testing, and qualitative fieldwork will be combined to examine whether the intervention increases civic use of Velin, reduces service failure, and changes younger speakers’ perception of the language’s usefulness.

The project treats digital language support as a matter of political power as well as technical capacity. Velin was excluded from Darskan public administration during most of the twentieth century, and compulsory schooling in majority-language Merec continued in the Estuary until 1987. Digital systems can reproduce that exclusion even when no official language ban remains. At the same time, collecting speech from a small population creates risks of surveillance, commercial extraction, and unwanted standardization. A Velin Data Trust and elected Community Language Council will therefore control research access, approve release of language resources, and retain the right to suspend data collection.

## 1. Background and rationale

Darska’s 2024 Household Language Count recorded 8,600 residents who use Velin at least weekly, 12,400 who understand it but speak it less often, and fewer than 900 speakers aged under twenty-five who describe themselves as confident users. These categories are imprecise, but the age gradient is consistent with local school enrolment and community-organization records. Existing preservation efforts have increased the visibility of Velin songs, place names, and ceremonial speech. They have had less success establishing domains in which a resident gains a practical advantage from using Velin.

Meanwhile, public administration in the North Estuary is being digitized. Six municipalities now direct residents to automated telephone menus before they can reach an employee. Five use appointment kiosks in service centres, and three are procuring text-based assistants for housing and family-support queries. Velin is absent from all but one of these systems. The exception is a telephone menu containing twelve prerecorded prompts, but users must switch to Merec to describe their request.

This matters beyond convenience. When a language cannot be used to report a broken heating system, arrange accessible transport, or ask why a subsidy payment stopped, speakers receive a repeated signal that it belongs to memory rather than public life. Younger or less-confident speakers may avoid it precisely where successful use would demonstrate its contemporary value. Conversely, adding a language superficially can be worse than honest absence: mistranslated instructions, unrecognized dialects, or a machine that fails without offering a person can increase both material harm and linguistic embarrassment.

Most digital preservation projects begin by asking how much text or audio can be collected. This project begins with a different question: **what institutional conditions make it safe and worthwhile to use a minority language?** It focuses on procurement because purchasing rules determine whose language is treated as a core requirement, what counts as acceptable performance, who owns resulting data, and whether suppliers must repair failures. Procurement is therefore a form of language policy, even when presented as a neutral technical process.

## 2. Research questions and hypotheses

The primary research question is:

> Does requiring usable, community-governed Velin support in municipal digital-service contracts increase the routine use of Velin in public-service interactions?

Four secondary questions follow:

1. Does the standard reduce task failure and unwanted switching from Velin to Merec?
2. Do effects differ by age, dialect, confidence, disability, or prior experience of administrative discrimination?
3. Does repeated successful civic use change whether residents regard Velin as worth learning and transmitting?
4. Which organizational practices—rather than speech-recognition accuracy alone—help or hinder adoption?

We hypothesize that municipalities operating under the standard will show a higher rate of completed Velin transactions than municipalities awaiting implementation. We also expect lower rates of language switching and smaller completion gaps between Velin and Merec interactions. Among residents aged sixteen to thirty, we anticipate an increase in perceived practical value and willingness to use Velin with children or younger relatives. We do not expect a 30-month intervention to produce measurable population-level language revival or fluent new speakers.

## 3. Conceptual framework: institutional usability loops

The project proposes an **institutional usability loop**. A person attempts to use Velin in a consequential setting. If the system understands, completes the task, and provides dignified repair when it fails, the interaction increases the person’s expectation that Velin will work next time. Visible use also gives staff and suppliers evidence of demand, which can justify further investment. Better provision then produces more opportunities for use.

A negative loop is equally possible. A badly translated menu fails; the user switches to Merec; low recorded use is interpreted as low demand; and Velin support is cut. Conventional usage statistics cannot distinguish lack of demand from demand suppressed by poor provision. The proposed trial intervenes simultaneously in technical performance, repair procedures, staff practice, and purchasing accountability to test whether that loop can be reversed.

Preservation is defined here as expansion of a language’s viable domains and the social expectation that it can be used without penalty. This definition complements, but does not replace, outcomes such as speaker numbers, proficiency, or intergenerational transmission.

## 4. Setting and partnerships

The study will include the eight North Estuary municipalities of Aven Quay, Belisar, Corren Fields, Dova Reach, Elwick Strand, Marden Fen, Orra Vale, and Ternmouth. Their populations range from 9,000 to 44,000. Estimated Velin-speaking shares range from 6% to 31%. All have agreed in principle to align a scheduled technology purchase or contract renewal with the project timetable.

Three bodies will share governance:

- **The Estuary Municipal Consortium** will coordinate procurement and staff access but will not receive identifiable research data.
- **The Velin Data Trust**, a nonprofit entity established before collection begins, will hold audio, transcripts, and derived language resources.
- **The Community Language Council** will comprise twelve elected Velin users, with reserved places for younger speakers, disabled residents, speakers of the inland and coastal varieties, and people who do not belong to existing language organizations.

Council members will be paid at the same hourly rate as specialist municipal consultants. The council may reject proposed vocabulary, restrict the release of recordings, require a system to be withdrawn from a service domain, or pause research collection. Municipalities will retain responsibility for delivering services and for providing Merec, Velin-speaking staff, and non-digital routes where applicable.

## 5. The Velin Digital Service Standard

The intervention is a contractual standard rather than a single application. Participating procurements must include six requirements.

### 5.1 Functional task coverage

Velin must support complete tasks, not merely greetings or navigation. A resident who begins a supported housing-repair request in Velin must be able to describe the problem, confirm details, receive a reference number, and understand the next step without mandatory switching.

### 5.2 Dialect-sensitive evaluation

Suppliers must test coastal, inland, and mixed urban Velin. Performance reports will be disaggregated by variety where sample size permits. The council will approve test sets and may prohibit publication of small cells that could expose individual speakers.

### 5.3 Dignified repair and human escalation

After two failed recognition attempts, the system must offer a Velin-speaking employee, a callback, or a structured non-voice alternative. It may not repeatedly demand that a user “speak clearly.” Users must be told when the system is uncertain rather than receiving a confident but potentially incorrect response.

### 5.4 Data minimization and non-extraction

Raw voice recordings may not be retained for product development unless a user separately opts in. Suppliers may not create voiceprints, infer identity from accent, sell language data, or use research material to train unrelated commercial systems. Contracts must specify deletion schedules and allow independent audit.

### 5.5 Community language work

Translation, terminology creation, testing, and correction must be paid. Suppliers must maintain a correction register showing which community-reported problems were accepted, rejected, or remain unresolved. Reasons for rejection must be provided in accessible language.

### 5.6 Public performance reporting

Municipalities will publish quarterly measures of task completion, escalation, abandoned interactions, severe semantic errors, and language switching. Word-error rate may be reported, but it cannot be the sole measure of quality because a single misrecognized address or negation can matter more than several harmless grammatical errors.

Before rollout, each municipality will select two or three eligible services. Likely domains include housing repairs, waste collection, concessionary transport appointments, local tax account queries, and childcare-subsidy scheduling. Emergency dispatch, clinical triage, policing, immigration decisions, and legal adjudication are excluded because failures in those domains would exceed the project’s initial safety capacity.

## 6. Study design

### 6.1 Stepped-wedge rollout

The eight municipalities will be assigned to four rollout sequences, with two municipalities entering the intervention every six months. The first six months will provide baseline data for all sites. By month 24, all sites will operate under the standard, followed by six months of observation.

Randomization will be stratified by municipality size and estimated Velin-speaking share. Assignment will be conducted publicly by an independent statistician after systems and services have been registered, reducing the opportunity to place technically easier services in earlier sequences. Municipalities cannot be blinded, but survey participants will not be told the rollout hypotheses.

The design was chosen because each municipality will ultimately receive the intervention and because procurement renewals cannot occur simultaneously. It also permits comparison of intervention and pre-intervention periods. However, neighboring residents may use services across municipal boundaries, and suppliers may improve later installations after learning from early ones. These processes will be measured rather than assumed absent.

### 6.2 Administrative and interaction outcomes

The primary outcome will be the monthly number of **successfully completed Velin transactions per 100 eligible service interactions**. A transaction will count as successful only if the requested task is completed or correctly transferred, the language remains Velin unless the user chooses otherwise, and no severe semantic error is recorded.

Supporting outcomes will include:

- proportion of interactions initiated in Velin;
- unwanted switching to Merec;
- abandonment and repeat contact within seven days;
- time to completion;
- human escalation;
- user-initiated correction;
- material errors, such as an incorrect appointment date or service category; and
- the completion gap between comparable Velin and Merec tasks.

Routine service logs will be separated from research telemetry. Residents may use a service while declining research recording. Opt-in telemetry will retain an encrypted interaction identifier, selected language, confidence estimates, repair events, task result, and user-reported satisfaction. Raw audio will be deleted within thirty days after authorized annotation unless the participant explicitly donates it to the Data Trust.

### 6.3 Resident panel

A panel of 1,200 residents will be recruited without using a government list of presumed Velin speakers. Recruitment will combine address-based sampling in the eight municipalities, open invitations through schools and community venues, and respondent referral capped at two referrals per participant. Sampling weights will adjust for recruitment route, age, municipality, and baseline proficiency.

Participants will complete surveys at baseline, 12 months, 24 months, and 30 months. Measures will include service use, language choice, confidence, perceived usefulness, trust in municipal systems, experiences of correction or ridicule, language use with younger relatives, and intention to learn or teach Velin. A rotating subsample of 320 participants will complete short scenario-based tasks, such as explaining a missed refuse collection or changing an appointment. Tasks will be scored for communicative success, vocabulary range, and willingness to persist after misunderstanding. The purpose is not to certify fluency but to detect changes in functional confidence and administrative vocabulary.

Participants aged sixteen and seventeen may enroll with assent and guardian consent. Because some households may disagree about Velin participation, communications will avoid labels such as “Velin household” on envelopes or shared devices.

### 6.4 Qualitative fieldwork

Researchers will observe procurement meetings, terminology workshops, service-centre work, and system testing. Eighty residents and forty municipal employees, translators, and supplier staff will be interviewed at least twice. We will deliberately recruit residents who oppose spending on Velin technology, speakers who prefer human service, and people who understand Velin but avoid speaking it.

Analysis will examine how “demand,” “accuracy,” “neutrality,” and “value for money” are constructed in decisions. Particular attention will be paid to moments when technical constraints conceal policy choices—for example, when a supplier labels Velin support an optional customization while treating Merec as part of the base product.

## 7. Analysis and statistical power

The primary analysis will follow intention to treat: a municipality is considered exposed from its assigned implementation date even if deployment is delayed or incomplete. A mixed-effects binomial model will estimate the effect on successful Velin transactions, with fixed effects for calendar period and registered service domain and a municipality-level intercept. Pre-specified interactions will assess age profile, baseline speaker share, interface type, and dialect coverage. We will report absolute percentage-point changes alongside relative effects.

A secondary dose analysis will use audited compliance with the six standard requirements. Interrupted trends for each municipality will be plotted to reveal anticipation, delayed effects, or abrupt supplier changes. Survey outcomes will be analyzed using weighted longitudinal models, while interview and observation materials will undergo framework analysis led jointly by academic and community researchers.

Based on a three-month feasibility audit, the included services are expected to generate approximately 58,000 eligible interactions during the study, of which 3% to 8% may be initiated in Velin at baseline. With eight clusters, four rollout periods, an assumed intracluster correlation of 0.03, and 10% missing outcome classification, simulations suggest 80% power to detect a relative increase of roughly 25% in successful Velin transactions. These estimates depend on stable service volume and may be weakened if municipalities select highly dissimilar services. The resident panel, allowing for 25% attrition, should detect a standardized within-person change of 0.18 in perceived practical value.

No single threshold will determine success. Results will be presented with uncertainty intervals, compliance data, adverse events, and qualitative evidence about why residents did or did not use the systems.

## 8. Ethics, political risk, and safeguarding

Language identity in the North Estuary is politically contested. Some residents view public Velin provision as restitution for prior exclusion; others regard it as symbolic regionalism or an inefficient claim on shared funds. The project will not require anyone to declare an ethnic identity. Eligibility for surveys depends on language experience or residence, and access to Velin services will not depend on research participation.

Small-language speech data can be identifying even after names are removed. Accent, family references, and place descriptions may reveal a speaker. Accordingly, audio will be stored in the Data Trust’s isolated environment, accessed only by named researchers, and reported through disclosure-controlled summaries. Publicly released resources will prioritize synthetic prompts, council-approved terminology, and short recordings whose donors have chosen a specific reuse licence. Withdrawal will remain possible until a recording enters an approved aggregate model.

The study will record and review adverse events, including incorrect service action, exposure of personal information, discriminatory staff response, systematic failure for a dialect, and distress caused by historical language questions. A safety panel with a council representative, a municipal safeguarding officer, and an independent digital-rights specialist may halt a service component.

There is also a risk that formal administrative Velin will privilege fluent activists or one prestigious variety. Terminology workshops will therefore begin with competing forms rather than a preselected official lexicon. Interfaces may accept multiple terms while displaying one plain-language explanation. Disagreement will be documented; consensus will not be manufactured where speakers genuinely differ.

## 9. Knowledge exchange and practical outputs

The project will produce:

1. a reusable model procurement clause for functional minority-language support;
2. an audit protocol covering task success, dialect equity, repair, and data rights;
3. a council-governed Velin administrative terminology bank;
4. de-identified test sets released only where disclosure risk is acceptable;
5. annual public hearings in each participating municipality;
6. supplier briefings and training for procurement officers; and
7. a policy report comparing the cost of meaningful provision with ceremonial or incomplete translation.

Results will be reported in Velin and Merec. Residents will be able to challenge interpretations before final publication, though no stakeholder will have authority to suppress unfavorable aggregate findings. Any licensing revenue from approved Velin resources will return to the Data Trust for language teaching, accessibility work, and future maintenance.

## 10. Work plan and resources

Months 1–6 will establish governance, register services, conduct baseline audits, and finalize measures. Months 7–12 will cover the first rollout, panel recruitment, and terminology work. Further rollout waves will begin in months 13, 19, and 25, with continuous safety review and public reporting. Months 31–36 will focus on final analysis, resource transfer, procurement guidance, and municipal continuation plans.

Resources will be allocated approximately as follows: 34% to research and technical staff, 21% to municipal integration and independent system audits, 16% to participant and council compensation, 11% to the Data Trust and secure infrastructure, 8% to interpretation and accessible materials, 6% to travel and fieldwork, and 4% to contingency. Suppliers will not be permitted to count routine contract obligations as research co-funding.

## 11. Anticipated limitations

The trial evaluates a bundled institutional intervention. If Velin use increases, it may be difficult to separate the effects of better recognition, improved escalation, staff training, publicity, or the political signal created by adoption. Compliance measures and qualitative process tracing will help identify plausible mechanisms but cannot fully isolate them.

Eight municipalities provide limited protection against cluster-level shocks. A regional election, service consolidation, supplier failure, or public controversy could coincide with rollout. Calendar-period adjustment and registered event logs will reduce, not eliminate, this problem. Cross-boundary use and supplier learning may also dilute contrasts between early and late sequences.

Finally, successful public-service transactions are not equivalent to language transmission. The study can test whether institutional usefulness, confidence, and administrative vocabulary change over 30 months; it cannot establish that children will become fluent or that speaker decline will reverse. Longer follow-up would be needed to connect expanded civic domains to household language practices.

## 12. Contribution

The project shifts minority-language technology from a question of whether a machine can produce recognizable words to a question of whether institutions can be held accountable for usable service. It combines a causal rollout design with community control of data, attention to dialect inequality, and direct observation of purchasing decisions. If the standard succeeds, the result will be more than a Velin interface: it will be evidence that procurement can create durable domains of language use. If use remains low despite safe and functional provision, the project will still distinguish lack of demand from failure of implementation and provide a basis for more honest public decisions about preservation.
